content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a HW/SW design space exploration framework for DNN compilation. Both the hardware architecture (buffer sizes, interconnect bandwidth, # PEs) and software (vectorization, tiling, etc) are searched iteratively using multi-objective bayesian optimization. A modified successive halving (SH) is used to hone in on a good SW/HW configuration. The authors observe that vanilla SH unnecessarily removed promising hardware candidates early and so they modified the algorithms to retain these candidates for the next iteration, to be evaluated with higher SW search budgets. Final selection is not based solely on performance or efficiency, but instead on "robustness", defined by the authors as low variation of performance with SW mappings at different budgets. In the evaluations section, the authors evaluate two accelerators, and compare to 4 search methods including HASCO that was published at ISCA last year.

- How does this work compare to SW/DNN codesign [1], and HW/DNN codesign [2]. I realize this work is different but it's perhaps useful to contextualize this paper w.r.t. to the mentioned works.

content.title: Response to reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks for your reviewing.

### 1. What other aspects of the presented algorithms are novel/new..?

The major innovation of UNICO is elaborated within section 4. To further clarify, we provide  a summary in below.

1) The major innovation of our work is an algorithmic framework for efficiently and effectively conducting a bi-level co-optimization (e.g. HW-SW co-design). This framework is a result of combining optimization methods from several different paradigms, including the multi-objective Bayesian optimization for hardware sampling, and the use of successive halving to adaptively conducting software search.

2) Within UNICO’s MoBo, we propose to sample a batch of HW configs to enable concurrent SW mapping search with the aim of increasing sample efficiency.

3) As you noticed, we further customized original successive halving (SH) and proposed modified successive (MSH) halving by improving the promoting candidate criteria. MSH is utilized to save search cost during each MoBo batch exploration. Please refer to Fig. 2.

4) The other novelty of UNICO is our adaptive MoBo surrogate model update mechanism. This approach identifies high-fidelity evaluated HW-SW samples in each MoBo trial and only use those to update MoBo surrogate model to ensure high approximation of joint HW-SW search space. This part is also a pure algorithmic innovation.

5) To improve HW design generalizability, we further relate it to HW configuration robustness to SW mapping choices. With that aim, we designed a *robustness* metric which alleviates the over-fitting of hardware to specific input neural network model. This particular concept and its formalization is introduced by UNICO for the first time.

UNICO integrates all these ideas together in a unified way, and is applicable to different hardware & software optimization scenarios regardless of the HW template, technology or environment. To demonstrate that ability, we utilized HASCO open-source backend for experimentation in section 4.1 and 4.2. Also, for a commercial case to show it practicality, we utilized UNICO on a commercial Accelerator co-optimization scenario in section 4.3.

### 2. About scope of our work: 
The major innovation inside of UNICO comes from its well-designed algorithm for the design space exploration. That is, we do not introduce new ideas on how to construct and model the co-design spaces (from HW engineering and architectural perspective), but focus on proposing a universal, efficient and effective optimization algorithm framework for accelerating neural network models. In this sense, UNICO might be more appropriately viewed as an ML application, rather than a hardware innovation research.

### 3. Some more comments on two mentioned work: 
[1] Turner et al. "Neural Architecture Search as Program Transformation" ASPLOS'21 [2] Abdelfattah et al. "Best of Both Worlds: AutoML Codesign of a CNN and its Hardware Accelerator" DAC'20. These works consider the problem of NAS. Although their application is within optimizing DNN accelerators, but they are fundamentally different from UNICO’s scope where we assume the neural network architecture and model are fixed.

### 4. Other approaches and why we focused explicitly on HASCO?
UNICO is a cost efficient yet robust bi-level co-search methodology that can be adopted for any co-design problem statement as long as it can be represented in a bi-level structure that is the case for HW-SW co-design. To demonstrate UNICO’s superiority, we chose HASCO, one of the most sophisticated and recent solutions, as one of our baselines. In HASCO paper, it has been shown that MoBo based co-search is superior to other search approaches including evolutionary (e.g. genetic).  To further see this, we also compared UNICO with NSGAII as an evolutionary rival, and a more sophisticated general algorithm namely multi-objective Bayesian optimization hyperband (MoBoHB), which also uses early stopping but is not specialized for the HW/SW co-design scenario.

(1) The paper lacks review/comparison with the most relevant related work, as listed follows. Please contrast/compare UNICO with the following work. (a) and (b) clearly tackle the same problem as yours. (c) proposes an offline solutions for designing accelerators and propose not only multi-model hardware optimization but also suggests the capability of their method to prevent overfitting.

[a] [Learned Hardware/Software Co-Design of Neural Accelerators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02075)

[b] [Data-Driven Offline Optimization For Architecting Hardware Accelerators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.11346)

(3) How different are the unseen models from the trained model? There are various ways to measure/quantify similarity between these models. That includes compute-/memory-intensivity of the models, or the type of operations each model has. Providing such details (or your intuition behind the way you created training/testing dataset) would be very helpful.

(4) Recent work suggested that infeasible design points are an inseparable part of hardware-software co-design. Have you observed (/consider) such design points in your search space? If not, what is your intuition on whether such infeasible design points would affect the performance of UNICO and how to extend your work for such realistic scenarios?

(5) In a more realistic setting, we generally optimize a hardware for a set of target models (that has multiple reasons including the costly process of hardware design). Do you optimize a hardware for a single model or UNICO has the capability to perform hardware-software optimization for a set of models?

(6) Can you provide additional details on your CA simulator? How long is the simulation time on average across the design points?

content.title: Response to reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks for the reviewing and pointing out some relevant work. We will add specific discussion to them in our paper. Here we answer the reviewer’s questions one by one as in below.

**Comment about Robustness:**
UNICO proposes the concept of HW generalizability to unseen app from the HW design robustness to promising SW Mapping choices, which is novel and has not been discussed in previous works. We explained our unique geometric way of quantifying robustness in our response to reviewer 2. In short, UNICO considers a HW configuration “robust”, when small variations in SW mapping parameters do not have high impact on PPAs. In other words, UNICO’s unique formulation and integration of robustness in HW-SW co-search avoid overfitting to certain type of workloads that appear at the time of co-search.

1. For a) and b), they are indeed are tackling the similar problem as we did in UNICO. However, UNICO is significantly different.  In below explain the differences one by one.

**[A]** Learned Hardware/Software Co-Design of Neural Accelerators This paper proposes a co-design algorithm framework with Bayesian optimization. The algorithm is a nested Bayesian procedure, i.e., the hardware sampling uses BO, and the software mapping optimization also uses BO. The advantage of this nested BO is justified in experiments by mainly comparing with random search or BO + random search. In practice, for example, it is doubtful whether using BO for software mapping search is the best choice. In fact, in FlexTensor (Zheng et al., 2020b), the authors have shown that a more carefully designed search paradigm performed better than BO for software mapping search. The baseline we mainly considered for co-design search is HASCO, where it employs BO for hardware sampling and FlexTensor for software mapping search. UNICO further advances HASCO by introducing a “successive halving” procedure for adaptively controlling how much to conduct the software mapping search (by FlexTensor) for each sampled hardware.

**[B]** Data-Driven Offline Optimization For Architecting Hardware Accelerators Different from UNCIO, which is a pure online approach, this paper presents an offline and data-driven method for predicting hardware accelerator for neural network models. It trains the prediction model by collecting a large dataset consisting of 452 million accelerator configurations. As explicitly stated by the authors of this paper, the goal of this offline-method is not to replace online optimization algorithms. Instead, it offers an alternative, and alleviates the heavy dependency of expensive simulator such as cycle-accurate model for optimization of hardware accelerators. In practice, it is desirable to combine both offline and online learning together. What UNICO offers is an efficient and orthogonal online optimization paradigm for this co-design optimization problem.

**[C]** Towards the Co-design of Neural Networks and Accelerators This work extends the capacity of traditional neural architecture search (NAS) by considering also the hardware parameterization in Google’s TPUs. The input is thus a problem (e.g. image classification) and a dataset, while UNICO is focused on optimizing the hardware configuration given fixed neural network models.

2. See response for reviewer 2.

3. The “unseen” models are selected by referring to the date they are released and the difference between the operator’s input dimensions (e.g. Conv 7D dimensions). That is, the training models are mostly models before 2018, while the “unseen” testing models are mostly after 2018. As per your suggestion, we added a discussion in Appendix to clarify this.

4. The existence of infeasible design is majorly a “framework” problem for the co-design paradigm. In our open source platform experiment, we use the framework provided by HASCO, where they employ a unified intermediate representation to effectively rule out infeasible designs. In our commercial environment with CAModel, the optimization is constrained by a set of parameters that’s unlike to be infeasible for input models. UNICO is more of an optimization algorithm, thus it does not explicitly consider the existence of infeasible designs during its search.

5. Yes, UNICO is used for both optimizing a single network model or multiple models simultaneously. E.g., for Section 4.2, UNICO is used to optimize four models at the same time.

6. CAModel is cycle-accurate model. It is a software to simulate hardware execution and provides accurate cycle counts, data transfer foot-prints, component utilization, etc. In our case, when it comes to commercial accelerator design cases, CAModel is very slow (i.e. price of being accurate), typically take minutes to even hours to execute one input model (depends on model size and structure). However, its result is quite accurate as it exactly simulates the behaviour of the hardware. In the related work section, we cited some open-source CAModels examples.

content.title: Thanks for the rebuttal
content.comment:
(1) Thanks for the clarification of prior work. However, I still believe that these work should be part of your review/comparison, and unfortunately was not covered in your revised paper.

(2) Regarding the search space, I don't seen that the rebuttal answers the question. How big is the search space? What is the total number of design points in the search space?

(3) I find the criteria for seen/unseen model weak. I believe that the release year can not be the sole criteria for this division. For instance, since self-attention was introduced in 2017, almost all the models use self-attention as their core operation. Elaborating on the type of operation between `seen` / `unseen` models would provide justification about the generalizability of your approach. As I mentioned in my rebuttal, compute / memory boundedness could be another criteria for dividing the models between these two categories.

(4) The statement is not entirely correct. The infeasibility can come from "framework", but it could be related to the infeasibility of hardware implementation or compilation stack. The existence of infeasible design points is indeed one of the challenges for hardware optimization. I am not trying to diminish the value of your work because of not covering infeasible points, rather, I am suggesting that infeasible points is an inherent characteristics of hardware optimization problems.

(5) Thanks for pointing out the multi-model search. I would generally refrain from calling them unseen models, MobileNetV2 and MobileNetV3 have pretty much the same operators. I instead suggest the authors presenting how much coverage the models in training / testing set have for example in terms of operation types. Do these models have mostly Conv operator? Do they have a new operator that testing set models do not have? etc. 

(6) Thanks for the explanation. Would it be possible to provide the average runtime of CAModel for few optimization that you have done? For example, in Figure 5 on average how long it took to run the simulations along with maximum simulation time?

content.title: Response to reviwer
content.comment:
Thanks for your careful reviewing. We clarify the reviewer’s concerns/questions in below:
* Search space: 
we conducted experiments in two settings. In setting 1, we use exactly the same search space as in HASCO. It consists of a hardware space and software mapping space. The hardware space is composed by choices of dataflows, parameters for buffer sizes, and processing elements (illustrated in Figure 1a). The software mapping space is composed by tilling choices (i.e. tile size and order) and parallelization for the loop representation of the given workload (e.g. Conv2D, MatMul, etc.). 

* SW Mapping Search Algorithms:
There are many software mapping search algorithms, for example, random search (used inside TimeLoop), genetic search (proposed by GAMMA) and etc. We used standard Flex-Tensor from HASCO as the software search (which behaves similar to a local search). The software mapping search is constrained by a budget, which is “number of iterations” or “number of evaluations”. The commonality of different software mapping search is that they are all “monotonic”, that is, given larger budgets, the best mapping found would never be worse. Given this observation, we thus propose to use “successive halving” to early stop some software-mapping search, avoiding to waste search budget when sampled hardware configuration is can be early identified poor.
* Performance Evaluation: 
There are different ways to evaluate the results of a co-design. In open source experiment, follow exactly as HASCO, we use MASETRO, which is a data-driven analytic model for estimation of PPAs. For experiments in commercial environment, we use a software simulator model (which is more accurate, but very slow) as the evaluation model. In all cases, UNICO and other algorithms are using exactly the same model for evaluation, and are searching on the same design space. Therefore, UNICO’s better results are solely due to its more efficient and more effective exploration behavior. In related work section, we elaborated on PPA estimation models and methods.
HW modeling:
This topic itself is a broad line of research and there are different ways to model a HW as explained above (e.g. analytical cost model, cycle accurate model). UNICO does not claim anything about a new HW modeling technique. However, we claim as long as a HW topology is modeled and there exist a huge configuration search space, UNICO is an efficient way to explore that space and find a generalizable yet optimum choice.
* Reproducibility:
Since UNICO is a modular bi-level HW-SW co-design solution which is not bind to a certain pre-requisites or environmental dependencies/constraints such as FPGA, ASIC, etc. authors planned to release the source code in near future for public use. That being said, we clearly provide all the details required for researchers to reproduce UNICO’s algorithm by using existing available libraries.

* Your question about “what is budget (section 3):
In UNICO framework, we have two types of search budget. First is MoBo trial search budget which is simply the number of iterations that we sample a batch of HW configs from MoBo surrogate model (Please see Algorithm, line 3). The second type of budget is SW mapping search budget which is frequently mentioned in section 3 and referred to as b. This budget is the number of times that we want to try a possibly better SW mapping configuration with a hope that the Power-performance improve. Simply put, depends on which search method we utilize (e.g. random, genetic, local), budget is the search budget in that concept.

* Figure 3 is a toy example for explaining our general idea and the difference of MSH with original SH. No, we select promoting candidates by combing AUC and terminal value (TV), as in Equation (1). For this example, the red one actually has the least preference w.r.t both TV and AUC, hence it was not selected.
We elaborate on AUC and F(Θ) in the next comment as per your follow up questions.

We’ll fix the typos; thanks for pointing out.

content.title: More explanation about AUC and $F(\theta)$)
content.comment:
* We clarify that our definition of AUC is **not** the area trapped between the curve and X axis. Instead, AUC is the area that is trapped between the curve and the horizontal line corresponding to the end loss value of the curve. 
Specifically, for this red curve you mentioned, the area is a *right-triangle* not a *trapezoid*. Accordingly, the $AUC=0.5(b1*(loss_0 – loss_{b1}))$, such that the red curve has smaller AUC than all the others because its $(loss_0 – loss_{b1})$ is smallest.

* According to the definition of robustness metric $R=Δ(1+F(θ))$, we consider a HW config *robust* if there is negligible (ideally zero) variations of latency and power when we select different promising SW mapping choices. That means, less $R$ means more robust so **the purpose of the search is to minimize $R$**.

To intuitively quantify $R$, we use Δ  to indicate the Euclidian distance between `orange` (relatively worse among promising choice) and `green` (best among promising choice) points, meaning if the $Δ=0$, then $R=0$. However, if $Δ>0$, we want to further consider the coupled behavior of latency and power; this is purposed by the second term $(1+F(θ))$. According to Fig. 4(b), if $θ=π/2$, that means latency was decreased by Δ and power was not changed, which implies power robustness but latency non-robustness with value of Δ. 

To incorporate this intuition in our robustness metric calculation, we defined $F(θ)=(6/π^2 ) θ^2-(5/π)θ+1$ such that $F(π/2)=0$, hence $R=Δ(1+0)=Δ$.

For the scenario when the `orange` point is in first circle quarter, $0≤F(0≤θ≤π/2)≤1$, the robustness metric range is $Δ≤R≤2Δ$. That means if $θ=0$, power variation value is $Δ$ and $F(0)=1$, hence $R=Δ(1+1)=2Δ$. This specifically implies our design prefer $θ=π/2$ more than $θ=0$.

On the other hand, when the `orange` point is in the second circle quarter, $0≤F(π/2≤θ≤π)≤2$, hence the robustness metric is further penalized to be within $Δ≤R≤3Δ$. The intuition behind this design is that from point `orange` to `green`, power was increased which is not favorable by our design in comparison to the other case (first circle quarter) when both latency and power decreases. That is, if $θ=π$, then $F(π)=2$, hence $R=Δ(1+2)=3Δ$.

* We will include these clarification in our revision.

content.title: power and latency for computing robustness metric
content.comment:
`Could we say your design emphasise power robustness more than latency robustness?`
Yes, the power change weights more than latency change.  The rationale is that latency optimization due to software mapping search is usually more sensitive, thus search results would tend to be more fragile if more weights are given for latency change. In some real-world settings, e.g., edge devices, power reduction can also be more important than latency.  

Thank you for pointing out the typo. We'll fix them in revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a Unified Co-Optimization (UNICO) framework for AI accelerator co-design, where as compared to the previous work, it can find robust accelerator hardware that generalizes better to new applications unseen in the co-optimization. Specifically, the major contributions can be summarized as follows:

    1. It proposes a batched hardware sampling strategy, to enable parallel hardware evaluation guided by multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) with a surrogate model that is refined with high-fidelity data samples selected by an adaptive data-driven approach

    2. It proposes concurrent software mapping exploration with successive halving for sampled hardware configurations, using a customized and effective candidate promoting criterion

    3. It proposes a method to enhance the generalization of hardware to unseen work-loads, by introducing an additional quantitative robustness measure into co-optimization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. They reasonably and, in my opinion, correctly identify the current automation/auto-search works issue on "generating a hardware for every single network"; it is not practical in reality

2. This work provide a clear formulation and algorithm illustration on how to optimize the hardware parameters for better generality.

2. They benchmarked a wide variety of workload.

Weaknesses: 

1. This work seems to mostly integrate the previous optimization techniques; I think the authors can more explicitly highlight their contributions 

2. The final performance highly depends on the hardware template a work assumes. The authors need to more explicitly confirm and elaborate that the baselines are conducted under the same or similar hardware template and search space.

3. Another major issue is that the results are only backed by the hardware modeling which may be not validated. I agree that during the search, it is not realistic to use hardware measurement or full-fledged simulation for all design choices. But after the search is finalized, a proper validation through hardware simulation or even measurement should be conducted to verify the hardware correctness.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the reviewing comments. We answer the reviewer’s major concerns in below:

1) UNICO’s innovations are elaborated in different places of manuscript including end of introduction and within section 4. However as per your suggestion, we revised the manuscript to make them even more apparent and we provide you here with some additional clarification:
 
**[i]** the major innovation of our work is an algorithmic framework for efficiently and effectively conducting the co-design search. This framework is a result of combining optimization methods from several different paradigms, including the multi-objective Bayesian optimization for hardware sampling, and the use of successive halving to adaptively conducting software search. 

**[ii]** We further customized original successive halving (SH) and proposed modified successive (MSH) halving by improving the promoting candidate criteria. We pointed out this innovation in section 3.1 and in Appendix B1, Fig. 6(b), we performed an ablation study to demonstrate the superiority of our proposed MSH vs original SH. We assume that the hardware space is given, and there is an existing tool to perform software mapping search. 

**[iii]** We further formalize the concept of HW design generalizability and further relate it to HW configuration robustness to various SW mapping choices. With that aim, we designed a “robustness” metric which in other words alleviate the over-fitting of hardware to specific input neural network model. 

**[iii]*** UNICO integrates all these ideas together in a unified way, and is applicable to different hardware & software optimization scenarios regardless of the HW template, technology or environment. To demonstrate that ability, we utilized HASCO open-source backend for experimentation in section 4.1 and 4.2. Also, for a commercial case to show it practicality, we utilized UNICO on a commercial Accelerator co-optimization scenario in section 4.3.

2) Search space: We used two setting for experimentation. Setting 1: we compare UNICO and HASCO exactly on the hardware template space defined as in HASCO paper. Setting 2: we adapt UNICO and HASCO for optimizing a real commercial hardware space, and use the same CAModel to evaluate the results. In both settings, all algorithms we used for comparison are exactly exploring the same search space. Their performance is thus only caused by their difference in optimization behaviour. Although we already referred readers to HASCO for extra information about those details and we explicitly mentioned certain template (e.g. GEMM HW intrinsic) we selected, we further added some of the important ones in our text.

3) Real-world application: While we did not prototype the results from HASCO hardware template space using real hardware, since we used the same backend as HASCO, our results are as legit as HASCO’s are. Moreover, our experimental results brought in section 4.3 based on CAModel are truly from real-world commercial setting, where a complicated software simulator cycle accurate model (CAModel) is used for evaluation. The CAModel is a popular choice in computer architecture research. The simulation there is expensive and accurate, i.e., each may take minutes to hours. Our experimentation took weeks to finish.

Other work: “EDD”, “AutoDNNChip”, “DNNExplorer”, and “Auto-NBA”. Co-design research have been a heated research direction especially in the industry. However, we note that these four papers are orthogonal to our paper. EDD proposes a differential method to conduct Neural Architecture Search (NAS) & hardware implementation of the network; they assume the hardware is fixed and try to search for a network architecture that best performance on that hardware. “Auto-NBA”can also be viewed as an extension of NAS. For “AutoDNNChip” and “DNNExplorer”, both are more of architectural paper, i.e., they proposed and designed different ways and frameworks to model the co-design space, instead of extensively studying how to explore these joint spaces efficiently. Our work does not include NAS component. We assume neural nets input models are given, and try to identify a hardware for efficiently computing these models. Our work is also orthogonal to “AutoDNNChip” and “DNNExplorer”.That being said, to further clarify the aforementioned differences, we added the above works to our related-work section.

We thank all the reviewers for their comments of the paper. To improve clarity, we have uploaded a new version of the paper with the following revisions: 

1. More description on the algorithm details are added in Section 3, e.g. illustration of how the AUC is calculated. 

2. Details on how the "seen" and "unseen" models are selected are added to Appendix. 

3. Typos are fixed.
